utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Registrar, and good morning to you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, distinguished gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And also good morning to the Defence team. In addition, Your Honours, this morning, this team will be enforced by a lawyer, Mr. Jose Doria with a view to the new coming witnesses, and also co-counsel Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to your team. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Vasvija Vidovic, with Mr. John Jones, appearing on behalf of Mr. Naser Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, as well as our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I take it there are no -- and good morning to you and your team. I take it there are no preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we can proceed and conclude with the cross-examination of the witness, and then start with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And may I say thank you for accommodating our request this morning that our client's family be permitted to follow from the public gallery, the minor member of his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That includes the minor, his son, because that requires my signature. I haven't signed it as yet, but I will --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It will be done during the break, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I will sign the document during the break because it was not available. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Jones: Continued

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We want to make a lot of progress today and finish with your testimony today, and I'm sure you want to go back to Bajina Basta and Cosici as soon as possible. So if you could please listen very carefully to my questions and just provide short answers, wherever possible, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when we stopped yesterday, I was asking you about Mehmedalija Tihic, and you confirmed that he had been injured on the road to Kolari. Now, my question is: You were asked about Mehmedalija Tihic when you were in Srebrenica as well, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told the people who asked you about Mehmedalija what you've told us, in other words, that he had been taken to receive treatment in Skelani or Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was exactly what I said, and that was true. I think it's reflected in my statement; namely, that in a location between Cosici and Kolari, Mehmedalija Tihic stepped on a land-mine and was as a result severely wounded. The people who were around took him away and transferred him to Skelani, and probably later to Bajina Basta, to receive treatment. I am not entirely certain about this, but I think that's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So that occurred before the 16th of January, 1993, Mehmedalija Tihic wounding himself.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I asked you yesterday whether the Muslims who had left your area tried to return. Isn't that what happened to Mehmedalija Tihic, that he was trying to return to his home when he got blown up in a land-mine?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with you. The reason is, those who wanted to leave their homes were escorted to Serbia, and I'm sure they're all alive and well where they are. Tihic was a renegade. He ran to the woods. He was part of the Muslim army. I think he was performing some sort of a check, or rather that's at least my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The point I'm getting at is this: You've repeatedly said over the last couple of days how you and other Serbs were simply defending your homes in Cosici. Weren't you, in fact, also trying to stop Muslims from getting to their homes, using land-mines, mortars, and other weapons to do so?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I can proudly state, yet again, that the only thing we did was guard our village. Tihic never passed our village; he didn't need to pass our village on his way home. The road led to Skelani, Bratunac, and the other villages. I'm not sure why he would have been coming from the direction of Kolari to begin with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, leaving that subject to one side, I need to go back briefly to something we touched on yesterday, and on Monday, when you told us that one reason why you thought that the Muslims had superior weapons to you was because they didn't take your cousin's rifle when he was killed. And my question is: Do I understand from that that you would usually expect attackers to take weapons from a dead enemy?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure you're getting my point. If you say that the Muslims were in the woods and that they were making a fire in order to warm themselves up - they didn't have a roof over their heads - who would have brought the weapons to the Muslims? A stork perhaps. Who would have given them the weapons, the means to attack my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was a different one. It seemed that when you were saying that your cousin's rifle was not taken by the Muslims, that you were surprised by that, and so my question was: Would you normally expect weapons to be taken from a dead soldier or village guard after he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I fully understand your question. But them getting weapons the way you're putting it to me, with some poles, I have no idea. They must have had weapons previously. As to what they actually picked up after he had been killed, that's a different thing altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you're either trying to avoid answering the question, or you have not understood the question. I'm going to put the question very simply: Was it -- it's being put to you that it maybe was the practice that when someone got killed and laid still with his weapon by his side, the attackers would take away the weapon. We're not talking of just your cousin, we're talking of every other -- was it a practice to take away the weapon as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one more question on that subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that something that you had seen before in combat operations before the 16th of January, 1993, weapons being taken from the dead?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I had seen nothing like that, the seizing of weapons. I did give you one example, the weapon I took from my cousin, for the simple reason that the weapon that was on him was much better than the one I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You told us on Monday that when your village was attacked you were "entirely surrounded." Now, that's not true, is it, because a way was left towards Skelani, and you drew that route for us on the map.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're trying to do. Are you trying to convince me that the village was not surrounded? My belief was that it would be surrounded, but it was, in fact, entirely surrounded on all sides. All the evidence you have demonstrates that they were even over there, at the bridge in Skelani, where they were killing the young as well as civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My point was this: If you were entirely surrounded, how did civilians evacuate to Skelani?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: It's really not for me to explain. There are people who died along the way, who were killed along the way, and I myself was captured. Everything that you're telling me now, everything you tried to tell me yesterday, you're not trying to convince me that I don't know the location of Maltasi. I had to pass through Maltasi four years in order to get to school. That was a much shorter route for me to take than down the river and across Arapovici and then on to Iljese [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, I'm not trying to convince you of anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't argue with the witness, Mr. Jones. Please, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm not arguing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Precisely why I told you next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not arguing. It's so the witness understands that I'm not trying to convince him of anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you went to Maltaska Gradina; so in other words, you went up a hill, didn't you, when you were withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. You're trying to sidetrack me, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't Maltaska --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, don't let me turn on you and censure you. I warned you yesterday, Mr. Jones here is doing his duty. If you were the accused, he would be defending you. So please answer his questions with a yes or no, where appropriate, and with an explanation where you feel it is necessary, but without any suggestions like the ones you have been making since we started the sitting this morning. You are being very aggressive this morning, and I won't let you remain so. I won't let you continue to be aggressive with the lawyer who is doing his duty here. He is asking you simple questions which are not provocative in the way, which are legitimate questions, and which you need to answer. I hope you have understood me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Maltaska Gradina a hill?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you went up that hill, you were more visible and vulnerable than when you were done in the valley; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't the reason why you went up the hill to Maltaska Gradina because you knew that there was a unit up there, a military unit?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't the reason you went up Maltaska Gradina because there was another unit there, and you were trying to join up with them?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was that I was heading in the direction of that unit. It was for my own personal safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But just to establish, wasn't that unit a special unit of the Yugoslav army; in fact, the Uzice Corps, which was up in Maltaska Gradina?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, it was just a village guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that that village guard, as you call it, had 5.56 millimetre American machine-guns and binoculars fitted with night-vision and a lot of special equipment not typical of a village guard? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you now about some prior statements which you gave about these events. You gave a statement, firstly, on the 23rd of February, 1993, to the Serb authorities, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll pass up, with the usher's assistance, copies of the 1993 statement in English and B/C/S. Just for the record, the B/C/S ERN is 02113343 to 02113345, and the English is the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, I'm going to ask you to look at this document, and there are a lot of details here which you've already confirmed for us, so I'm going to ask you to please confirm with a simple yes or no the following facts: First, after your release from custody, you were married but had no children and were living in Bajina Basta; is that true?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, was your address Rodoljub Colakovic number 8?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'll ask you to look at the first two paragraphs of that statement, starting at the beginning and ending with the sentence "I dropped the bomb and then I could not find it among leaves," which is a detail which you agreed yesterday. If you just glance at the first two paragraphs. I'll give you a minute or two just to read the first two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that I did, indeed, say everything you just told me, the way you've put it to me, and it sounds accurate to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of this interview, the 23rd of February, 1993, you're the only person in the world, I imagine, who knew that you had dropped your grenade and couldn't find it among the leaves; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, what I said is that I dropped it as I was trying to activate the grenade that my cousin had held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you have understood the question. The question that was put to you was a very simple one, again. It's being put to you that until you told these people who were interrogating you about losing your grenade, dropping it and then you couldn't find it, no one except you knew about this incident, about how you lost your hand grenade and you couldn't find it. It's only you who knew it, no one else could know it. Because the other person who was with you, in the meantime, was blown up, so there was no one else who could have possibly known this incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Da.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask that this be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. We're talking of a statement allegedly given by the witness on the 23rd of February of 1993 to the representative of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's the Republika Srpska ministry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior, Public Security Station Skelani. The B/C/S version consists of three pages, starting with ERN 02113343 and ending with 02113345, and the corresponding English version, which consists of four pages. This document is being tendered and received and admitted as Defence Exhibit D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, D169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 169, all right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more questions for now, Mr. Ivanovic, on this document. Is it right that the hamlets of Dvizovici and Kolari were on the other side of the hill from Maltasi; is that true?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's on the other side of the hill, Kolari specifically. I think they lie on the same plain, so to speak, in relation to Cosici and not on the other side of the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Mitar Nikolic from Kalamanci?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of a water mill belonging to Milan Nadvizovici, Kolari area?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I do know Milan from Kolari, down by the river, the river that runs past my village, if that's the water mill you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So he has a water mill, Milan.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was just one family there, and they lived in the water mill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember saying that the commander of the prison where you were kept was a man called Zele?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a man called Zele?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a man who had only one arm, was missing part of -- one of his arms?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw a man like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember telling a story which we see on the second page of this document, and I'll read into the record, it's ERN 02113344 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, incidentally, while you're reading from this document, I'm noticing, Mr. Jones, and whoever can check from the Prosecution side, that apart from these three pages that were just -- that we've just admitted into evidence, being the alleged statement of the accused mentioned before, and starting with ERN 0343 and ending 345, at least I have also an identical copy of the same statement. To be honest with you, I haven't gone through it in great detail, but I don't see any noticeable differences. In fact, I think it is identical. But it has a different ERN number, and it is basically a continuation of the previous one. It starts with 346 and ends with 348. Is there an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't have a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not at all. Perhaps we could have a copy of that at some stage, and we can see what it's about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can make it available. Perhaps -- I'm sure that in your records, Ms. Richardson --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, I was speaking with the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure if you look at the ERN number 02113346 to 3348, you should establish whether we're talking of the same document or not, and in that case, why we have two photocopies of the same document with two different -- with two different ERN references.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will check on that immediately. And I also, looking at this statement, I don't see Mr. Ivanovic's signature at the bottom. But we'll see what the last three pages are. It appears as though these -- someone took the statement from him, or someone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's not make comments. I just asked for verification of why do we have a photocopy -- two photocopies of the same document with two different reference numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We'll look into it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all. Because if there is a difference, then, of course, maybe Mr. Jones would like to tender the other copy as well. I don't know. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can look at it over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivanovic, do you remember telling a story, which we see on the second page of that statement, and I'll quote: "After an exchange took place for their nine dead and one alive man, this person stated that they had tortured him in Bratunac, that he had eaten oversalted pork, that he had been in mud up to his knees, they had cut his ears with a knife, that they had singed his body with a hot iron and made him to eat mud." There's a similar story in your 2002 statement. Do you remember that, that there was an exchange, that a Muslim came from Bratunac, he told stories, whether true or not, about his treatment? Do you remember that story? Do you remember that happening?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No, this isn't true. Some of the statements contained therein are true, but 90 per cent of it isn't. And, if you'll allow me, I'll explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's take it one step at a time. Was there an exchange, and did a Muslim come back from Bratunac, i.e., having been held by the Serbs, and tell stories about how he had been mistreated?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A young man was exchanged perhaps at the time when some Serb women were supposed to be exchanged. This young man was exchanged at Skelani. I heard that he actually originally came from Bratunac and was exchanged in Skelani for the women that I've already mentioned, and some other men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort of statements did he make, whether they're true or not, about how he had been treated?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of it I mentioned myself. When he was brought to the cell where I was held, he started explaining in front of the guards there how the Serbs had tortured him in Srebrenica, that he stood in water up to his knees, that he was forced to eat oversalted food and other -- and was suffering other types of torture. At that point, as I've said -- if I may explain, can I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one detail. You said the Serbs had tortured him in Srebrenica. Did you mean to say Srebrenica or did you mean to say Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I've never said that. I've explained how it was that it came about for him to be exchanged for the women and a few men in -- from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, it's just to correct something in the transcript. It says that this man said how the Serbs had tortured him in Srebrenica. Did he say how the Serbs had tortured him in Srebrenica or how the Serbs had tortured him in Bratunac? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he was tortured in Bratunac, of course, not in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, going back to this statement, it's written here: "After this statement by this man from Bratunac, 'prison became hell for us.'" My question is: Is it right that the treatment which you received became a lot worse after this man came from Bratunac, after this exchange?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, much worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in other words, the treatment which you received was not exactly the same the whole time you were in Srebrenica. It became worse after a certain point.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I was never really able to distinguish whether the times were easier or harder for us initially or at a later stage, except, of course, for the part that I spent at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this exchange, when this man came from Bratunac, can you estimate roughly when it was? Would it have been around, I'm suggesting, the 6th of February, 1993, i.e., 10 days or so after you arrived in the prison, the second prison?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I was never able to date it precisely, but I always said, and I think this is contained in this record, that it must have been halfway through my time in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a further couple of matters with this statement, but the question I'm going to ask you I want to preface by going back to Milomir Djukic in the hospital. And you told us how Milomir Djukic, at one point, was standing at the window, looking across to the PTT building, and he said, "Look, Naser" or "Naser Oric is leaving with five or six of his men." You told us that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And that's how I put it, I believe, and I've heard it from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you could look at the last page of that document in front of you, and it's page 3 for us, 02113345, there you describe how "the main liaison centre was located in the post office across the street from the hospital." And then if you can see that in the statement, [B/C/S spoken]." Do you see that near the top? Check?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the next sentence you say: "Naser is escorted by his men, about four or five policemen. He wears a white leather jacket with dark stains on certain parts." And my question is: That refers, doesn't it, to this incident you've described of Mr. Djukic seeing the post office and describing that scene; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with a description of his clothing. I know what I said, and I stick to that. At no point in time was I able to actually stand up or sit upright in bed and look out the window. I merely conveyed to you what Djukic told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's simply to make this point: That in the statement, when you say that Naser is escorted by his men, about four to five policemen, that was referring to a sighting of Naser Oric from the hospital leaving the post office.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you want me to explain, I can, I mean what he told me. But at no point in time that I say that I ever saw him myself, because I was not able to get up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. That's completely accepted. My point is this: That looking at your 1993 statement, apart from this mention of Naser Oric as seen from the hospital, you never state, do you, that you saw Naser Oric in the prison, in this statement.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know him in person. I told you that those were my assumptions in the prison based on what I heard from other people, and I believe I never maintained otherwise in relation to my testimony about the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Now, in that statement, you also said that Muslims were planning to attack Bratunac or Ljubovija "unless they received some help and food." My question is: Did you understand that at the time the Serbs in Bratunac were blocking food from entering the enclave?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of any such thing, nor was I able to state any such thing, of me knowing that somebody was planning to attack Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're dealing with the food situation. Did you not hear at any time that there was a food crisis in Srebrenica, and that that was possibly why the food that you received was so terrible, because there was very little available?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this was quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, on the last page of this statement, there are a number of details of an intelligence nature. I'm going to put each one to you and see whether you remember saying it or whether you agree. Firstly, that at that time, one kilogramme of tobacco cost -- it says, "BM 1.000," perhaps that's -- well, do you remember how much a kilo of tobacco cost?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I myself could not know this. I heard this from soldiers who were shouting out after Ahmo Tihic had tobacco with him, and I heard that they basically mostly smoked raspberry leaves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that Monday was market day at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you remember that the kitchen, or a kitchen, was in the basement of the department store? In fact, I think you mentioned the department store, on Monday, being across from the SUP. Do you remember that detail?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I never made any statements about the kitchen. I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was a journalist in Srebrenica from Germany and that he had been wounded in the arm?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Dr. Ilijaz from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. And this is precisely what I stated. If I may expand my answer a bit. I would have wished to have known some of them, because they were so kind to us, at least for the duration of my stay at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that one of them had come from Tuzla into Srebrenica, one of the doctors?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. As I've said, I don't remember these people. But I don't believe that I ever said anything bad about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not suggested that you did. On the first page of that statement, it appears you gave some information about Marko being called Mico. Do you remember a Marko?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember Marko. I know that he got killed on that bridge. I did not know him in person, or anything else about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Kano, do you remember someone called Kano? My apologies, Cano.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If you mean Cane, many people are called by their name, and perhaps you have a totally different person in mind. Perhaps if you could tell me what this person did before the war, then I might be able to tell you something about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. For the moment I've finished with this statement, and we can put it aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I would have a question with regard to the statement. Mr. Ivanovic, you have been captured the 16th of January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And you have been exchanged on the 26th of February; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, the statement you have been asked for by the Defence, it's stated from the 23rd of February. That means that it was taken or made before you were exchanged. Do you remember that you made a statement to some people of Republika Srpska before you had been exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, may I, just before the witness answers, there's another date as well which appears, on the 27th of June, 1993, a prisoner exchange took place. It may be that the person who put this together was clumsy about the dates. I certainly wouldn't want this witness to be under the impression that this statement suggests he was interviewed before he was exchanged. It's clearly an error, a typing error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But I think it should be made clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've asked -- I've gone to some considerable length, and in fact I cut the exercise short, to establish details which only this witness can know, a very painstaking process, I might say. And if Your Honour's purpose is to shed doubt on this document by virtue of a typing error, I hardly think that's unfair to the Defence. I would note that these questions are never put to the Prosecution; they only seem to be directed at us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: No, I was just wondering how it can happen that the statement said he was exchanged at the 26th of February and the statement is dated on the 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a typing error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the 27th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My suggestion is it's a typing error, and I don't think this witness can help with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Another question. Does the witness -- a couple of minutes ago, when you have been asked with regard to what happened -- what you had been told by one of the other prisoners, you told us that 90 per cent of this statement is not true. Now, what did you refer to? Did you refer to the whole statement which you had allegedly made, or did you refer to the statement made by the other prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the statement, a lot of what the person had said was true. But I believe in my statement that I gave, I explained rather well how it all went, and what this person said upon his arrival to the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, do I have to understand your testimony this morning that 90 per cent of this statement is not true, and you want to go on to explain why it is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly. I wanted to explain the matter in my own words, because I don't believe I myself could have stated it that way. Perhaps somebody has made additions of their own. Perhaps someone -- if someone was adding anything to this statement of mine at a later stage, I, of course, would not be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I feel I should pursue some further questions, then, about this statement. A lot of the details have been confirmed by the witness, and it seems I should go ahead and confirm further details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a Vasiljevic, who people in Srebrenica asked you about, as being some sort of militia commander?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Vasiljevic? My apologies, I'll withdraw that. It's not so much a question of whether you were asked about him. But have you ever heard of a commander Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember being asked about Buko or Buco committing -- Buco, committing robberies around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, there's a reference to a Pira or Piro, who I think you mentioned in relation to your exchange. So do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know him well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what his role is, or what his role was at that time, who he was and what he did, any details about him?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you frankly, he never came to my village. What he was doing in Skelani, I really don't know. I only know about him coming to my exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you know him well, so surely it wasn't just on that one occasion that you saw Piro.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I used to see him earlier on, because Piro, the one I know, if we have the same person in mind, his mother worked at the school that I frequented. He has a twin brother. And there's no reason for me not to know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's his full name, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Branislav Gligic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that Branislav Gligic was not Piro and that he was not at the exchange.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I really don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can come back to that. Now, do you recall making a statement in September 1994 about these events?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. Perhaps I was undergoing treatment in that period of time. Perhaps somebody was asking me questions and then putting them down on a piece of paper, but I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll pass up copies so that you can have a look, with the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And, for the record, the English ERN is 03092377 to 03092381, and the B/C/S -- one moment, please. The B/C/S is 00652255 to 00652261.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could look at that, Mr. Ivanovic, do you agree firstly that that's your signature at the foot of each page?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: That's what my signature should look like, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you can probably confirm the following with a simple yes: Isn't it right that you trained to be a plumber in Belgrade, that you took up employment in the Prajd Montaza enterprise in Belgrade, and that you were on a job in Tivat in Montenegro when the war started. Can you confirm all those details?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It's not that I was offered the job, I had already been working on that post for ten years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your wife Nada Jevtic from the village of Bozici?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 16th of September, 1994, were you still living at the same address, Rodoljub Colakovica number 8?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I lived there, but I also went to see my mother and father at Cosici. But actually it wasn't really my place of residence, because I did not really have a house of my own. I just had a part of my brother's house for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at this document, do you accept that this is your statement, the statement which you gave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it directly. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think in all fairness we have to give him an opportunity to go through it, Mr. Jones, before he can answer the question in a reliable manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Can I make a practical suggestion, in lieu of saving time, that if I ask for an exhibit number for this statement now, I can then ask some other questions, and then perhaps during the break the witness can look at the statement. I don't know if that can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And perhaps I can add to that. Will you be also making use of other statements that we have?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, one final --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I suggest is that you ask the basic questions that you can proceed with and not requiring the witness knowing the details of these statements, and then we'll have the break and make them available to him so that at least he will have read them before he can answer further questions from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. At any time we can have a break. I mean, we are not bound by the 10.30 time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My only concern is timing, and the Prosecution were more than six hours, as I mentioned, and I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not restrict. You don't have to worry about that, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The only thing you need to worry about is what we're worrying about; namely, that I wouldn't like to allow questions to be put to the witness on the contents of this and other statements which he has never seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I share that concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And in addition, I would like to ask the witness, when you read this statement during the break, that you in particular also read the last paragraph in the statement where it is said that this statement was dictated aloud for the record, that "everything I stated was entered into it," and that you did not wish to read the record, that you also take notice of this statement at the end of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say, with the utmost respect and some regret, that I know Your Honours wouldn't want to be seen to be prosecuting this case. If Your Honour is inviting the witness already to take note of a point which might provide him with a means of escaping from his statement which he may not want to admit is his own, then I think this is unfair to the Defence. I'm sure these are points the Prosecution can take in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it can be taken that way, Mr. Jones. It is obvious that we are drawing the attention to a part of the statement on which there will be a question, and I think we can leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can I just that a Defence exhibit number be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll start with the alleged statement of the witness in B/C/S, consisting of seven pages, starting with ERN 00652255 and ending with 00652261, and the corresponding English translation of the same, consisting of five pages, starting with ERN 03092377 and ending with 03092381.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other statements that you would like to tender, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it's an October 1994 statement, and the ERN in English is - I think it's the same as the B/C/S - 00652238 to 00652240.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, the first one that we have just referred to will be marked as Exhibit D170, and the one I am going to give the details of now will be -- is being tendered, received and admitted and marked as D171. This is a statement alleged to have been made by the witness, consisting, in the B/C/S version, of three pages, starting with ERN 00652238 up to 00652240, and the corresponding English translation of the same, consisting also of three pages, with what appears to be the same ERN number. This is a statement which purportedly was given by the witness on October the 16th, 1994, to the main judge of the court in Zvornik -- in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivanovic, as you've, no doubt, followed, you'll have an opportunity to see these statements over the break, so for now I'll just put a couple of points to you. Firstly, with respect to the statement dated September 1994, I put it to you that no where in that statement does the name Naser Oric appear, anywhere. That's something which he can't answer now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he can't answer that now. Unless he's given an opportunity to read this statement, he's not in a position --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can take a break now then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to make that exact point that you just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can safely have a break now rather than later. We'll give him the opportunity to -- do you want him also to have available the statement he gave to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So, Mr. Ivanovic, I am giving instructions to the staff to make available to you the copy of these two statements. Please read them carefully, because you are going to be asked questions by Mr. Jones later, and perhaps also by us. Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we can proceed. I want to make sure, before we proceed, Mr. Ivanovic, that these documents were handed to you, and that you had an opportunity to go through them during the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, let's start with the September 1994 statement, D170. It was pointed out to you by His Honour, Judge Eser, before the break that in the last paragraph, it stated that the statement was dictated aloud for the record, "everything I stated was entered into it." Isn't it right that this statement was read to you so that you had an opportunity to correct anything which was wrong or to add anything which you felt should be added?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I really can't remember this, although maybe up to 90 per cent of what it says in here is precisely what I experienced. But in one of these paragraphs, for example, there is a reference to Mico's last name, which I, in fact, never knew. I didn't even have his name on that list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, can you confirm that the name Naser Oric, or even Naser, doesn't appear anywhere in that statement?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I've read the document and I didn't see that the name was noticed. I think I -- my heart was at peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. At the time you gave this statement, you knew who Naser Oric was, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did say that a number of times. I didn't know the man, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to distinguish between the time when he was in detention and to make sure that he's understood your question, at the time he made this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I have a number of questions in that regard, if I may follow on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let you proceed. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, coming to that. Isn't it right that, in fact, you didn't mention Naser Oric because you were never sure - to this day you're not sure - whether you ever saw him in the prison? It's only an inference you made.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I could only assume, during my captivity in the cell behind the court building, that was based on what I heard from the soldiers. But I did not know the man personally, nor can I say that I recognised him in the reception room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And today, sitting there where you are, you can't say for sure, can you, whether you ever laid eyes on Naser Oric in the reception room in the prison.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I've said this, haven't I? I really didn't know him. I have confirmed a number of times that I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, leaving that statement to one side for the moment, the September 1994 statement. Looking at the October 1994 statement, do you recognise your signature at the bottom of each page of that statement?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: By looking at the signature, it looks very much like mine. It's nearly identical. Now, as to whether I signed this or not, I really -- but I can't challenge the fact that I signed these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree that in that statement, too, there is no mention of Naser Oric, in the October 1994 statement?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my reading of the document, I don't know whether there is any mention or not. I simply don't remember everything. But as I went through the statement, I gathered that it contains a lot of what I knew. There are a number of details that I'm not sure about. I don't think I spoke about specific names or anything like that at the time, at least to the extent that I remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to make it very clear that we don't challenge that you were beaten in Srebrenica and that it was a horrible experience; I want that to be a hundred per cent clear. What we do say is that Naser Oric was not in the reception room in the prison. That's what my questions are concerned with. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I fully understand what you mean. As I have said, I don't know him personally. I don't know if he was there. But I think I've explained with sufficient clarity what my assumption was based on. But I did say a number of times that I simply didn't know whether it was him or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Your assumption was based on what the guards said; correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move to another area altogether. Well, not altogether different. Just sticking with the meeting in the reception room, was it right that Ratko Nikolic was there at the same time as you, when you were brought in to see the five men?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Rade Pejic and Ratko Nikolic were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you were also by His Honour whether the dark-bearded person resembled Mandza, and you said that he didn't. It's right, isn't it, that you knew this person as Mandza, not as Hazim Mrki from Voljevica; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Your reference to this man from Voljevica, this is something that I never said. I met Mandza, for the most part, during my exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, really, I want to make clear that Mrki is another -- there's a Mrki Mandza and there's another Mrki. Now, I want to stick with these statements again for a bit longer, and in fact, if you can look again at your 1993 statement. Now that we have them as exhibits, there are some points I want to raise. Do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Does he have the 1993 statement, D169.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I do have a couple of additional questions about this meeting in the reception room of the prison. Can you estimate roughly when that took place? And if you can't give us a date, perhaps you can tell us how long it was before you went to the hospital, for example.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. The only thing I can remember is that it was halfway through my captivity, and it was around noon, that's what I'm trying to say, the questioning. But I couldn't give you the exact time. Given my condition at the time, I don't think that I can be expected to have known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly not. But would you say it was shortly before you entered the hospital? Was it a matter of days before you went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Will Your Honours bear with me for a moment. I may be able to save some time by revising some of the questions I was planning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You can, in fact, put the statements to one side for a moment. I may not ask you about them again. I'm going to move on to the question of the injuries you sustained in Srebrenica. And I apologise if it's painful to go over it again, but I'm sure you understand that I have to. Now, you told us yesterday that when you arrived at the SUP, right at the beginning of your captivity, before the 40-day period even started, that you were already "less alive than dead," those were the words you used. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that. My condition was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I could take it step by step. First, you were bloody, weren't you, because Mile's grenade detonated, injuring you.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. But at the moment I was injured, I don't think I was bleeding all the way to Srebrenica, before I was beaten the next time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mile right next to you, or at least a few metres from you, when his grenade detonated?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I've described that already. He was lying down on his stomach over the ditch, and I was lying down on my back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't the force of the blast so great that it actually threw Mile's body across the stream where you were?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you're saying about this stream, but perhaps I can provide a more practical explanation. It was a ditch, and the distance was, for example, between me where I'm sitting now and the next table. And there was a path or a road, and that was the same distance, roughly, across that ditch, and that's where we were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. My point, really, is this: Is that wasn't that a great explosion that went off, sending shrapnel, that is, pieces of metal, into the side of your face and the right-hand side of your body?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably like that, if it forced his body across the creek. I was injured myself. This is easy to prove. I simply grew numb instantly, and my arm and my leg were bleeding. As for shrapnel that struck Mile, I think most of the shrapnel actually hit his stomach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then when you were captured, the soldiers kicked you in the mouth, among other things. Weren't you bleeding from that injury as well?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember clearly. I know that someone struck me in this area, and from behind my back, someone struck me or hit me with a rifle butt, spat at me. I have explained this a number of times. Whether I was bleeding as a result of that, too, at the time, I really can't say. I do know that I was bleeding profusely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, didn't an old lady come out and beat you with metal tongs? And my question is: Didn't she beat you around the head with those tongs?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: The blows that the old lady dealt me in a village -- well, she probably set out to crack me over the head, but she probably missed and struck me in the shoulder instead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally again on the truck you were beaten even more by soldiers with their rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to summarise, before you even arrived at the SUP, you had shrapnel injury to your head, right arm and leg, soldiers had kicked you in the mouth and hit you with their rifle butt, and an old lady had hit you repeatedly, and then soldiers had hit you. Is it right that you were a bruised and bloody mess when you arrived in Srebrenica on that first night?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I've described in detail how everything happened on the lorry, and I told you who was the most assiduous beater. I did tell you that I was slapped, spat at several times, they lit a match, "to see the Chetnik," as they said. And they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it also be right to say that it was mostly local Muslims, local from your area, who mistreated you the worst, and not just on your day of capture but throughout the whole time you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. That man beat me on the lorry. I didn't know the man, but those were not significant injuries, in a manner of speaking. If those had been the only injuries, I would, indeed, have been a very lucky man. I would even kiss him if I met him now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I said, not just on that day. When you were in Srebrenica, weren't you mistreated by a Budo who from Dobrak, so in the Skelani area?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the lorry, nor did I ever say that he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not in the lorry. Later, when you were in prison, didn't someone from Dobrak particularly mistreat you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I did point this out a number of times. I heard people talk about this man, referring to him as Budo, Purta or Senad. I couldn't be sure whether he was from Dobrak, but later on, I sort of inferred that this man named Budo was from Dobrak, as I have said. I didn't know this man personally either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't he mostly beat you, Budo? Most of the beating you received was at his hands.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. He was the one who beat me the most, and he brought in little girls who were lighting pieces of paper. There would be a heap of small pieces of paper under the table the next morning. And while he went about beating us, the girls were laughing. That was my explanation on Budo, if you have the same person in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you told us that, and there is no need to repeat anything you've told us already. I'll just be asking you quite short questions, and you can give short answers. Isn't it also right that the injuries to your nose and cheek, the fractures, were inflicted by Dzemo Tihic, who was a former neighbour of yours?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, he broke my nose bone. I did say repeatedly that I believe he was the one who broke my cheekbone, too, and then the beating continued several times later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why my question was, taking the whole time that you were in captivity, wasn't the worst treatment you received from specific individuals who were from your Skelani area?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to say. I told you about arriving there in a lorry. There were many people beating me. And what I told you about, Dzemo breaking my bones, I started bleeding at the time. Whether it was at the time, I really can't say. But I do assume that he was the one who broke my nose and cheekbones. I'm telling you this exactly as I experienced it at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you a little bit about the SUP. When you arrived at the SUP, there were people in civilian police uniforms, weren't there, wearing the old Yugoslav police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. There were people wearing those uniforms too, most of the people that were there, at least to the extent that I was able to see that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the SUP you told us you were beaten by Muslim women, men, girls and boys. Is it right, then, that people could just come and go into the SUP, especially at night, that they could just enter at will?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't agree with that, that women and children would come in at will and beat us. I believe I provided a detailed description. Some of them did come, but maybe some of the policemen were there too. What I know about the very early hours, when that man grabbed me by the ears and hit me through the bars, those people who came with him, I saw clearly that they were in civilian clothes, and some were in camouflage uniforms. Now, who allowed them to come in, I really don't know how they got to us. But I did say clearly that they did not come into the cell. They would grab us -- grab me by the ears and hit me through the bars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as you know, is it right that the front door of the SUP was not locked so that people were coming in and hitting you through the bars because they didn't have the key to get into your cell? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've described this. The cell had bars, and there is a wall there. They didn't enter the cell. I described exactly how they hit me. But if you want me to go through this again, I'll be glad to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm going to move on now to the second place you were kept, and I'll call it the prison, just for -- to keep it short. You referred to that prison as the national defence building, or the All People's Defence building. That was the name of the building before the war, wasn't it, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. Someone probably told me, and that's how I knew, and that's how I referred to it. Now, whether it is the All People's Defence building or not, it's really not something that I can know. I did say many times -- how many times I've been to Srebrenica previously, and what the reasons had been for me going there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the people at that prison were also in old police uniforms, weren't they, or some of them.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of them. They were wearing different kinds of clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that at that time you thought that Mandza was the person in charge of the prison? That was the impression you had.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: What I want to say is I did not know this man Mandza previously. What I'm saying about him is from the moment I learned who he was, and this was the early stage of my exchange and when I was taken to the hospital, and that's all I can speak about. Anything else I would tend to disagree with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm looking at your 2002 statement, and it's paragraph 171 just for our reference, ERN 01171390: "Mandza seemed to be in charge of prisoners. I think he was some type of commander." So wasn't that your impression at the time, that Mandza was the boss in the prison?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't believe I could have stated anything like that. Again, I'm telling you, I did not know Mandza. I think I explained this with sufficient clarity, when it was that I met Mandza. And later I realised, and during my last exchange, I already knew him quite well and we exchanged greetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. And if you could please keep your answers short, because we're all keen to make progress. There's no need to repeat anything you've said already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have an objection with respect to the paragraph that was just read by Mr. Jones. I think Mr. Jones has made the reference "Mandza seemed to be in charge of the prison," the statement says "Mandza seemed to be in charge of the prisoners." I think that's an important point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I heard Mr. Jones saying. I mean, I stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think -- when I read what he said, I read verbatim what was in the statement. I asked him whether he had the impression that he was the boss of the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My hearing is usually not defective in the least.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My objection is being in charge of the prison is one thing, being in charge of the prisoner is something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I never heard Mr. Jones suggest to the witness that he had said that Mandza was in charge of the prison. What I heard Mr. Jones saying was, suggesting to the witness, that in his statement he had stated that Mandza was, in his opinion, in charge of the prisoners. I may have heard --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if that's the case, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, dealing with the beatings which you received in the prison, I think you've told us that you were beaten mostly at dusk, you said 9.00 or 10.00 in the evening. So it's right, isn't it, that it was very dark at that time?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that everyone in your cell was beaten at night?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: More at night than by day. I believe that's what I said originally, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But isn't it right that Milomir Djukic was in your cell for two days at least, and that no one beat him?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for two days, precisely. For two days he wasn't beaten by anyone, and then he was returned to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the beatings were occurring at night, when it was dark, how did Milomir Djukic manage to avoid getting beaten, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he told me so himself, after we met again at the hospital. I don't believe I saw this myself, because my condition was very difficult. I think I've described this, haven't I? I never said that I saw this with my own eyes, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was in the cell the same time as you, wasn't he, Milomir Djukic?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But as I said, for two days only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that Ratko Nikolic didn't get beaten that much. And again my question is: How is it possible that he had a differential treatment when you were beaten when it was dark? How was he singled out for less severe treatment?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea why, or how. I know that he was standing near the door, if you want me to go through that again. I really can't give you the reason why his treatment was what it was, why he was beaten less. I have been able to explain exactly how many times I've been stabbed by a knife, and exactly what they did to me. If you want me to go through that again, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's no need for that. Yes, Mr. Jones, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Simply to make this point: That you told us how in the evening you would hear trucks stopping, people saying, "let's get the Chetniks," running into the prison and then beating you. You accepted that it was dark at the time. So my question is: How did Ratko Nikolic manage to escape such a severe beating if you were all being beaten by these people in the dark?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to explain is this: Why was that? Ratko Nikolic was standing next to the door, and the first thing they would say when they came in is, "Who is Ratko Mladic?" And then he would hold out his arm with two fingers raised, and then on their way in whoever came in first would whack him. I'm not going into that again, because I believe I provided a description of that already. And then what happened later, they started lighting those pieces of paper and they started beating us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, the guards at the prison, you told us, provided you with a stove, which I think you said they filled several times. Wasn't that to keep you warm? And didn't they also try to block the window to keep the heat in?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. Do you want me to explain?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why would they --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've explained this, haven't I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained that the guards provided you with a stove, and that they filled it and lit the stove. Surely that was to keep you warm.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that. In that case, they wouldn't be pouring cold water on us, they wouldn't beat us, and they would not stop up the stove-pipe that was going out through the window. There was no glass pane in place there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to read something from your September 1994 statement. It's page 4. The ERN is 03092380. You don't need to refer to it because you've told us something similar here. You said: "From time to time, I heard the sounds of women crying in pain and dull blows coming from their room, but I cannot say anything specific about any abuse or maltreatment they suffered." So do you say, do you maintain that you heard the sound of blows, i.e., people being hit in the women's cell? And again, you can provide a short yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard -- based on what I heard, the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I put it to you, Mr. Ivanovic, that not a single woman was mistreated in that prison, and that you've simply said that because you're prepared to say anything about how mean the treatment was in the prison, no matter how untrue. That's my suggestion to you.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you understand me, if you understand my description. I heard a voice, but I never, for a moment, suggested that I had heard blows or any sort of noise. I said there was a voice. Whether it was someone moaning or not, I really can't say. I really can't describe the voice for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I've read from your statement where it says "dull blows." Here you told us: "I suppose we were beaten more often and more severely than the women," by which you were implying, weren't you, that the women were also beaten?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely what I'm telling you. I heard voices. Now, if they were beating them or not, I really don't know. Maybe someone said differently, or that I indeed stated that they were beaten with pieces of wood or bats. I don't think I ever said that. I did speak about a voice that was sort of prominent, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, please --

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe there was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- keep your answers short. So is it right, then, that you didn't mention hearing blows coming from their room, and so therefore the ICTY investigator either misheard you or added that to your statement?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can only answer the question by saying this: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you spoken to Svetlana Trifunovic since you've both been released?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No, we've never spoken. I did pass her in the street several times, but I never spoke to her about her [as interpreted]. And the reason was that she used to come to our prison and spit at us on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not important. Have you spoken to any of the other women who were held captive at the same time as you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever spoken to Branko Mitrovic, who you mentioned on Monday?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I never spoke to Branko either, but I heard that he himself had said that he had not been beaten. And, as I've told you, I heard him play in the corridor with some other children. I think I've described it well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you've been -- since you were released, have you ever met and spoken with Branko Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: With Branko Nikolic, no, never on that matter --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Mitrovic, yes. I did meet with him, but I never discussed these matters with him, nor go beyond that which I remember myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
