utterances.text: In your 2002 statement, and it's paragraph 138, you said: "Branko LNU and Svetlana Trifunovic were detained in the cell together with the women." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Branko? I apologise, I'm a bit sleepy. I haven't had five hours of sleep together. This is a very difficult experience for me, going back to that time. So if you don't mind, can you please repeat the question, and I'll answer it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. No problem at all. And if you need a break, I'm sure Their Honours would be glad to give you one. It was simply this question: Do you remember saying that Branko was detained, detained at the prison, with the women?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. He never was, because I know that from the very start he was held with us. And he can confirm that himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if that's in your 2002 statement, that's something which is not true. All right. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If Your Honour will bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just a few more matters. As far as nutrition is concerned, I think you told us that in all the 40 days you were imprisoned, you ate and drank practically nothing, and that you only went to the toilet once. Do you maintain that?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Food was, in fact, brought twice a day, wasn't it? And what was brought was what everyone was eating in Srebrenica, including the guards; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you that I was speaking for myself. Perhaps the food was brought over, but I did not eat it because of all the beatings I had to endure. I really can't remember how often they would bring the food in the course of the day. I know that I didn't eat it. I remember that once this woman came and placed a plate on my chest. But even then I was in such a bad condition that I couldn't eat. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had no water for 40 days?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did drink water. But I think I explained it quite clearly what sort of water it was. It was full of feces, urine. And they told us to drink it, they were calling us Chetniks, and that they weren't there to serve us, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, perhaps from your time in the hospital, that there was no clean water supply in Srebrenica because the Serbs had destroyed the water treatment plant and therefore everyone had filthy water. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'm going to ask about some of the other people you were in captivity with. Firstly, the people who were brought in from Cerska. And I'd like you to have a look at the note which you produced, I think it was, yesterday, P474.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's P475.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies, P475.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, according to that, Mico from Sase was brought in from Cerska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was brought over from Cerska, but I remembered Mico simply as Mico from Sase. And I believe I explained that quite clearly as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You have no idea what Mico's real name is, do you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, weren't the people brought from Cerska in a terrible condition when they arrived because of what they had suffered from anything from five to seven months in a stable near Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When they were brought over, they were not in a condition that was as severe as ours, although later on it all seemed to be kind of presented that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they arrived, they were already bloody, apart from Andza. The men were already bloody, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: At that point I never saw Andza. She was probably put up together with the women. I explained to you when it was that I saw Andza, and what she told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The men, the men were already covered in blood when they arrived at the prison, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were probably covered in blood, beaten up, but they were not in as severe a condition as I was, by the look of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree that some or any of them were already close to death when they were brought in?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't agree with that, not at the point when they were brought in. I remember well that they stayed on after I left for the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's start with Jakov Dzokic. You last saw Jakov Dzokic alive, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know, do you, if he died, or if he did die, whether he died in the cell or at some later stage?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: After my exchange, I never heard of the man again. I only said that I knew what his condition was when he remained in the cell after I was transferred to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Rade Pejic after your release?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that Rade Pecic, and that's how I had his last name written down, I never knew the man before. I can only tell you about him from the time that we spent together in the hospital, but nothing else. I heard that reportedly he went out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. My point, really, is this: You don't live anywhere near Jakov Dzokic, do you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You seem to have assumed he died because you didn't see him again. But would it be normal for you to bump into Jakov Dzokic, in the normal course of things?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard specifically that he was alive, but I'd really like to know if he is. I heard that he was thrown out of Srebrenica by the Muslim defenders. Now, that's just what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't the same true of Dragan Ilic, that you last saw him alive and you don't know for sure what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what happened to him later on. I only know that he remained there. Not knowing anything about him, I might have stated in my statement that he might be dead. But I stick to, therefore, what I said, either this way or the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, you stick to not knowing what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for Mico, we've seen a Mico who appears to have come in from Cerska. Wasn't there a Mico in the SUP when you already arrived? I'm looking at the transcript. It was the 24th, Monday, page 34, line 12: "Then there was Mico," and in the context, that is, of when you arrived. So was there a Mico in the SUP when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe that's what I said, that Mico was at the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you also say that there was a Mico who was brought in to the second prison with Cane and Miloje Radanovic. And I'm looking at your 2002 statement, paragraph 69: "I'm not exactly sure when, but three more other Serb men who had been imprisoned were put into the cell with the five of us. I will tell you what I know about the other three men." And then paragraph 70: "FNU, LNU, called Mico, born in 1950, from Sase." And then in the next two paragraphs you mention Cane and Miloje Radanovic. So is there another Mico again who was brought in with those two men?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could remember, and on the basis of what I had in writing, I knew about this one Mico. I don't remember the other one. I could even describe the man to you. I know the disposition in which we were lying on the floor in the cell at the All People's Defence building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mico, you told us that he died after he was beaten by a 16-year-old boy who was asking where he had hidden flour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I don't know if I said that he was a 16-year-old boy. I might have said that he was perhaps 16 to 20 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was a young man or boy.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: He was very young. That's why I described him that way, at least as far as I could see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to someone who you knew as Kojo. It's right, isn't it, that you don't know what his name is. You don't know yourself what his full name is.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't know him before. I met him the moment we got into the prison, and I explained and described him to you, to the extent that I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'll refer to him as Kojo. Didn't he die after this exchange which occurred with the Muslim man coming back from Bratunac, after a particular beating on that evening, which I put is the 6th of February, 1993, when a bunch of people came into your cell and beat all of you? In other words, wasn't it that specific evening, a beating of that specific evening which led to his death?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say, really. I did explain to you clearly that we were beaten every day and every night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't there a particular occasion when there had been an exchange and this man had come back from Bratunac, and also bodies had been returned from Bratunac, and that a lot of Muslim civilians got very angry when they saw the state of the bodies and rushed into the cell and attacked all of you? Do you recall an incident of that nature?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about this. I only know about this young man that I was telling you about, when he got into our cell. And then this other man who came in and said that, although we are Chetniks, he wouldn't hit us for the whole of Srebrenica. I've explained it quite clearly. You can take a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I say, there's no need to repeat anything you've said already. Didn't, on that occasion, or indeed on other occasions, the guards sometimes try and stop people from beating you?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No, that never took place. I assure you, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, how much more do you reckon you have? The reason is my attention has been drawn by the Victims and Witnesses Section to see whether it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can certainly pause now. I probably have another half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me put it to the witness himself. More or less, we have about half an hour left. We can have a break now, if you want, or we can finish with your testimony and then you can go. You told us a few minutes ago that you are feeling a little bit tired because you hadn't slept enough. If you think you need a break now, and we will resume and then finish half an hour later, we can do that. What do you think? What is your preference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd prefer to finish my testimony now. I will do my best to endure this, because I would really like to finish this and go back home. I fear that my condition could get worse if the situation is prolonged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Jones, and let's try to finish by -- the next break will be at 12.00, not at 12.30. We are flexible. Instead of 12.00, it would be a few minutes past 12.00, but it's not the usual 12.30. That's because we resumed after the first break earlier than -- half an hour earlier than usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time. I'm not, in any way, interfering or suggesting that you should shorten --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, I understand that. I'm confident I can finish my 12.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And please understand, Mr. Ivanovic, I'm not trying to put you through an ordeal, and there will just be a few more questions. All right. I want to ask you about Branko Sekulic. Now, you last saw Branko Sekulic alive in the hospital, didn't you, being taken care of by doctors and nurses who were doing their best for him?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Sekulic? Yes, he was with me at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the hospital, didn't the doctors do their best for you, all of you, including Branko Sekulic, giving you pills and injections and attending to your injuries?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody was dressing our wounds, to the extent that I could see. I did tell you that we were administered some injections; I don't know what their substance was. We were given some pills. But I can't say whether it was these treatments that helped me and the others recover or rather simply the fact that we were not being beaten anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctors were doing their best to keep you alive, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I'm grateful to them, and probably the others, those of them who have survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the hospital, wasn't Branko Sekulic alert and able to talk, because he was providing information to Milomir Djukic, just as you and Rade Pejic were?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, basically, all of us were conscious when we got to the hospital, although we could not get up. And Branko Sekulic could stand up, although he had to be given some sort of a staff to assist him to walk to the toilet. I think I've already explained this clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hadn't Branko already been injured before his capture, if he told you, in Rogac.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. I assure you that he never mentioned Rogac, nor did I write that name anywhere. This is the first time I hear this. I don't have it in my notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I want to fix, if possible, the dates and times that you were in the hospital. I know it's difficult. But you mentioned yesterday, I think, that you were interviewed by a person who you thought was a judge. Now, can you, first of all, try and fix that for us, how many days that was into your captivity, how long before you went to the hospital, how long after the incident where Rade Pejic's beard was burnt? If you can fix it in relation to some event, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I wish I could do that, but I was in such a bad shape that it's difficult for me to date individual events. I relayed these events as best I could. I wasn't able to find out what the date was. It was difficult to endure this ordeal for one day, let alone 40.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, leaving that meeting aside, I want to clarify one point about the meeting in the reception room, if you can go back to that. And I believe there may have been a misunderstanding. You seem to be telling us that when you were brought into the reception room with the five or so people, that you were lying down in front of the people. Now, is that correct? Or were you, in fact, standing up when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I never said that. Nobody forced us to lie down on the floor. We were standing in front of them, and they were deliberating amongst themselves, asking some questions. I never said that we were prone; I simply said that we were lying down when we were being beaten. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Believe me, Mr. Ivanovic, that's what I understood you to be saying, but there was a mistake in the -- a mistake arose, and so I'm glad you clarified that for us. Now, Ismet Hodzic was in that reception room, you told us. Didn't he help to get you transferred from the prison to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me that I never saw him at the time. When I was transferred down there, as I've already been explaining, it was -- the course of events was that we -- there was simply this truck that came to pick us up, although I don't even remember that. I remember that we were walking up the staircase, and that then I found myself in the hospital room. I was even telling you about the soldiers assisting me to go up the steps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And if we are to finish by 12.00, Mr. Ivanovic, if you could keep your answers short. I'll try and ask you very specific questions. My question, really, was this: Didn't you understand at some point that because Ismet was grateful to your father, Radenko, for helping him, that he helped you to be transferred to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure that this is true. I'm grateful to Enis and to his family, and I even visited his family. This was the man I mentioned that came, visiting me, to the hospital and at the prison. I don't know to which extent these people are to be thanked for some things. I only know that I was done in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just two more areas I want to cover with you. Regarding whether Ratko Nikolic was in the hospital with you, I think it's fair to say that we have different versions of whether he was or was not. In your 2002 statement, you say repeatedly that Ratko Nikolic was in hospital with you, and I'm referring to paragraph 172, at page 18 of 27, quote: "All four of us, Ratko Nikolic, Branko Sekulic, Rade Pejic, and I were put into the same room at the hospital." And then it goes on, at paragraphs 172 to 220, to state that you were in the hospital, you and Ratko Nikolic, you went for an exchange, you came back again. I understand now that you're saying he wasn't ever in the hospital with you. So is that right?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't remember this particular detail. Perhaps I might have said one thing and then something else was added, although I'm not blaming anyone for this. I only remember that I was taken to the hospital, and that there was this truck in front of the court and the municipal building, and that they were going to fetch this Ratko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did each time you went for these exchanges, they would take you from the hospital and then Ratko Nikolic from the cell; and then at the end of the first two failed exchanges, take you back to the hospital and Ratko Nikolic back to the cell?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that's how it happened. I'm not sure whether this is true or not, but at least that's how I remember it, how I explained it. I remember well the course of events during that first exchange, when I didn't even believe it was going to be an exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it right, then, that Ratko's condition was not so bad that he needed to be hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I know Ratko very well, and when we were exchanged, Ratko was in a much better condition than I was, physically speaking. However, psychologically speaking, he was much worse off, because he was unaware of things, he seemed to get lost, at least as far as I remember in relation to the first exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he know that you were in the hospital when you were going for these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. Honestly, I'm telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Rado Pejic, how long was he in the hospital with you, more or less, if you can estimate?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He was there from the moment I was brought. How long he stayed after I had left, I really can't say. And what we said about him a while ago, asking whether he was still alive or not, this is something I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were exchanged, you and Ratko alive, that was for dead Muslims, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Two dead bodies and two persons who were alive, to the extent that I could see. There was a coffin placed on a cart. When I was being taken there, I couldn't walk. And there was quite a lot of snow, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Did you see two live Muslims coming back from the other side when you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. They sat on a coffin. You know what I mean when I say "coffin." It's something with bars. I'm not sure how to explain it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what final area, and it concerns this, document P475, if the witness could be shown it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, please. Do you still have it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to clarify, do you say this was copied word for word from the note that was written down by Milomir Djukic?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I left home, on that list that I told you about, on one side I wrote down people from Cerska and on the other side the people from Skelani. It was just a note that I made to keep myself from forgetting, and that's what I'm telling you. It's in my wallet, and before I left to give testimony, I copied it so that it may serve as a reminder in case I failed to remember some things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in fact, isn't there another piece of paper, which is what Milomir Djukic wrote down, Milomir Djukic, which you then took with you and which you, in fact, gave to the Serb authorities and did not retain?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the Serb authorities took that from me or whether it was something that I copied from one of their documents later on. But I have this well-warn piece of paper that I have on me. By the time I got there, I couldn't remember some of the details, such as whether it was given to me. This is all I can tell you about that. I still have the same list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's just to establish, the list which Milomir Djukic wrote down, which you then hid in the hospital and, I think you said, in your cell as well, that list you gave to the Serb authorities after you were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say whether I did or not. What it says there, I really can't say. I can't challenge the fact that I may have given it to them. But maybe it was something that I copied from one of their documents later, in a bit, to learn about the fate of those people, or maybe somebody brought it over to me. I really don't know what I may have said at the time, or how I gave it to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your 2002 statement, page 25, ERN 01171397, paragraph 248: "Djukic gave me the list. I hid the paper in my underwear. When I was exchanged, I still had the paper with me. I gave the paper to the Serb authorities sometime after I was exchanged, and they kept it." So could that be correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I really can't challenge that. I simply don't remember what exactly happened in those days. I can only confirm what I still remember, but I can't challenge the fact that I may have given it to someone in Skelani, whoever happened to be there. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one final question on that document: You told us that you didn't believe, when you were being taken for exchange, that you would be exchanged but that you would be killed. Why did Milomir Djukic give you a list, this precious document, and why did you accept it, if you really feared for your life?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I simply didn't know that I would be taken to be exchanged in the first place. He didn't give it to me at first because it hadn't been written. I think that was written after the first or second day there. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- you also told us that you went back to your cell, and that you were trying to hide the piece of paper in your cell, placing it beneath the linoleum. So did he give you that document before you went for exchange or before you went back to your cell? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to clarify this. I never said that I hid that piece of paper in the cell. What I tried to explain was that I took out this piece of cloth from my underwear which are used to make a noose. The idea was that I would hang myself before they started cutting me up with their knives. There was a table in that room and some pipes from which I intended to hang myself in the case. I never said that the list was hidden there. I believe my explanation at the time was quite accurate and detailed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's really just to make this point, Mr. Ivanovic, and it's my last question: That isn't it right that you really didn't fear that you would be executed when they took you to hospital and that you didn't fear certain death if returned to the cell, because if you did fear either of those things, you wouldn't have taken custody of this precious list but you would have left it with Milomir. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was your answer, if there was an answer? And if there was a question, because actually it was more of a remark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: When you took this piece of paper with the names on it, you didn't expect to die, did you, you expected to live and be able to pass that paper onto someone.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't know that I would make it. He wrote this down for us so that we could -- it's as simple as that, just in case any of us survived. But it wasn't out of the question that I could perhaps survive, or any of us for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Try to finish in less than 10 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will. Re-examined by Ms. Richardson:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, you were asked about whether you told the investigator or whether you told anyone in 1994, when you gave your statement, that Naser Oric was being present. Do you recall being asked that by Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please just repeat this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I'll rephrase it. When you were interviewed by the investigator, were you asked about putting together the face that you saw in the room in Srebrenica, where you were interviewed by the five men, with the face that you saw later on as you watched television?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm afraid we're talking about a statement from September 1994. We've got no evidence at all of when he saw television programmes. It was a matter I didn't get into because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a matter that you didn't get into, but it's a matter that he testified upon, and he never said when.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To avoid confusion, if we can at least, first of all, make sure the witness understands he's being asked about September 1994, and when he allegedly saw photos of Naser Oric. Otherwise, I think it may be confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that needs to be cleared up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Your first question, in any case, needed to be re-put in a different fashion in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interests of time, I'm trying to speed up. I'll take it one step at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll take it one step at a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, you recall that when you were released from prison, you said yesterday, as you testified, that you observed the person that you believed was Naser Oric, and you saw his face on television after you had been released; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did see the face, but I believe I've explained this in great detail. I tried to learn as little as possible about anyone in order not to remember all these things about my captivity, to remember as little as possible. As for that person, I assume, based on the talk at the reception room -- and I do believe that I did see him in at least one other place, that person, but I never said that I was certain about that person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, my question is this: Were you, in 1994 -- had you seen the image? Do you remember exactly when it was that you saw the face of Naser Oric on television or sometime after you had been released?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or in newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or in newspapers.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him a number of times in the papers and on TV. I can't give you the exact dates. I never needed to memorise those. But, of course, I did see his face on TV, in the papers, as their soldier. But I don't think I can talk about that, I can only talk about what happened to me from the day I was captured until my release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But since your capture, 11 years have passed, plus, almost 12 years. When you maintain that you saw pictures or images of Naser Oric on newspapers or on TV, relatively speaking, approximately, was it at a time soon after your release, your exchange, or was it in recent years, that you saw his images on TV and on newspapers? We would like to know. And the reason why we would like to know, I will tell you later. But for the time being, you need to remember, try to remember at least, when was the first time that you saw an image of Naser Oric on TV or on a newspaper? How many days, months, years maybe, after your exchange?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, after my exchange, I saw that face, but I can't remember the dates. I can't say, for example, I saw that face on such and such a date. But I do remember all too well that I saw the face on TV, where he was made out to be a soldier. And I saw his face in the papers too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if I put it to you that you were released -- exchanged in 1993, would you accept that, during that same year, in 1993, you had already seen images or photos or pictures of Naser Oric on TV or newspapers, in that same year, or would you exclude it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I, to the extent that I remember, I really can't say. But it occurs to me now that I may have seen the same person in the newspapers after my captivity. As for the exact time period, believe me, after I had been released, I was not even allowed to eat on my own without medical supervision. I really don't know when this may have been. I did see him with those same clothes, and just as I've described him to you. The person that I saw at the reception room, that I had been taken to from detention, he had long hair and a beard. But I really can't say anything else. Nor do I want to necessarily link this up with any images that I may have seen later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will leave it at that, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just because it's such an important point, it's very clear there's never been any recognition, any recognition, by this witness of Naser Oric. He made clear in cross-examination that the inference was based on what guards said. I certainly avoided asking 20 or 30 questions about identification which I would get into if that were ever in issue. It isn't, and I suggest we move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure the Prosecution would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In fact, the record is clear that the witness stated that he -- at the time that he first saw this person with the beard in the room, he didn't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but anyway, no arguments in the presence of the witness. If you have more questions, please put them. I'm not going to proceed with any questions, further questions, on this matter with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I don't know I would get anywhere and I don't think I should try to get anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and the record speaks for itself. Thank you. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivanovic, the individuals who beat you at the national defence building, Tihic, you knew him from before; correct?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Tihic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And at the time that he beat you in the national defence building, as far as you know, was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this person Budo, who beat you as well, was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the others that you described who came into the cell, were some of those individuals who beat you soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's for sure. Most of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, could we have clarification of which Tihic? Because there was Ahmo Tihic, there was Dzemo Tihic, there was Mehmedalija Tihic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to, Mr. Jones. We all know which of the Tihics. It was certainly not the one --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's Dzemo, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the Tihic that he mentioned before anyway, one of them, because there was another one who stepped over a grenade and ended up in -- Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And just very briefly, Defence Exhibit 169, I would just have that handed to the witness for just a couple of questions. It won't be very long at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a statement that was assigned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Supposedly the 23rd of February, the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. ERN number 02113343, that's the English, and then the B/C/S version 02113346. And I should also say, Your Honour, with respect to your question about the various -- the different ERNs, it is the exact same document. We were able to verify that during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. So we'll ignore the other, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, could you just look at the last page in that document, and tell me if -- I should say, if you sign -- if you recall signing this document at any point. Is your signature on this document in the B/C/S version? Do you recall signing it?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's, for the record, not there. My next question to you is: Do you recall advising -- do you have any recollection of this person Osta Bozic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ostoja Bozic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the name that appears on the last page of this document. If you look at the document for a moment, the last page.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I can look at it if you want me to, but I'm trying to listen carefully to what you're asking me, because I don't know if there is a person by that name in Skelani at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Because that is the only way I could know the person. I don't know of this person, so I don't think there's really any need for me to look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That answers my question. Do you recall telling, or giving information that you had been a member of the Skelani battalion? Do you recall, in 1993, telling anyone that?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is really something that I don't remember. I've clarified this sufficiently, as to where I was, and that Kojo was with me. But they were perfectly within their rights to call me whatever names they liked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document also states, "on June 27, 1993, a prisoner exchange took place," and that -- I won't read the full statement, but it appears as though this document is stating that you were exchanged on June 27, 1993. Is that information correct? Or were you, in fact, exchanged on the 26th of February?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that really matters. I don't think that really has anything to do with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time. It's obvious that this statement contains a lot of inaccuracies. I mean, even the day of his capture --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I thank you, and I was just making --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's the only inaccuracy, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 16th February. But it couldn't have been taken on the 23rd of February either, if he was relieved -- released on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Someone could have been careless with dates and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In the interests of time, I will not go through all the other inaccuracies in this document. I have no further questions for Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Judge Brydensholt would like to put a question to you, or more than one question. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Well, I go back to the moment when you were brought to this reception room in the prison. First of all, were there other prisoners present at the same time?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. Before we were transferred from the police station, I hadn't seen anyone else there prior to that. I hadn't noticed anyone else in that cell. The first people to be brought in were the group of people who -- that were transferred from the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Please, this is a misunderstanding. I'm thinking of the time when you were brought from the cell to this reception room. Were there other prisoners brought at the same time to the same reception room, or were you the only prisoner present in the reception room, for the investigation?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There were some, myself, Rade Pecic, and Ratko Nikolic, the people who were brought there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes. Were you all there during the same period? When you were finished and brought back to your cell, were the other prisoners brought back at the same time?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice anyone else being brought in, or taken back to the cell, or rather the reception room. My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were there, the three of you were there, during the same period, and when you left, the other prisoners left as well?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that. The other prisoners came to the reception room later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: So you were not there at the same time?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean, "at the same time." I explained that I had been -- the three of us had been taken out, three of them, and there were between five and seven people there. I'm not sure what was recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies, I think I've mixed this up a little. When they took me out, you're talking about the people who were already at the reception room when I was being interrogated? Is that what you have in mind? Because I started talking about when they were beating us. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes. I'm speaking about the meeting where five persons were present in the reception room. They were asking you some questions regarding your military career, and that kind of thing. And I'm asking you, at the same time as you were examined, were there other prisoners in the same room, in the reception room, to be asked questions?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was the only person brought to the reception room, at least as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And for how long time did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: Not for long. A handful of words were exchanged, but many of them kept silent. At once they said, "Take him back to his cell." Two soldiers escorted me back to my cell, and that's all I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: But did I understand you well that you had the opinion that the meeting was dealing with whether or not you should be exchanged? Is that what you are telling me?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think that was the subject of their discussion. Much later, I was eventually taken to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes. But what was the subject of their discussion then, if it was not regarding your exchange?

utterances.speaker: Ilija Ivanovic [resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea why they came to the reception room. As I have said before, I think it's on the record, they asked me several questions, then they said that I should be taken back to my cell, and that was that, as for that particular meeting, if you like. If you want me to go again through what I could hear while there, I can do it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: No, thank you. I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Do you have any questions, Judge Eser?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: The questions that I have had are already answered. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I don't have any questions for you, Mr. Ivanovic, which basically means that your testimony comes to an end and you are now free to go back home. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, on behalf of Judge Eser, on my own behalf, but also on behalf of the Tribunal in general, I should like to thank you for having accepted to come over and give testimony in this case. And you will now be assisted by Madam Usher, who will escort you out of the courtroom to another room where you will receive, from now on, all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home. Once more, I thank you, and behalf of everyone I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for hearing me out. My best wishes to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now we will have a 25-minute break, and then we will start with the next witness, all right? Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's wait for the accused. Yes, everything is in place. Good morning, Mr. Dzokic. I am the Presiding Judge. My name is Carmel Agius. To my right I have Hans Henrik Brydensholt from Denmark, and on my left I have Judge Albin Eser from Germany, and I come from the island of Malta. I would like to know, first and foremost, whether you are receiving interpretation in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you think that the volume in your headset is either too low or too high, please let the usher know and we will make the necessary adjustments. I would like to welcome you to this Tribunal on behalf of the Trial Chamber, and also on behalf of the Tribunal in general. You are about to give evidence, which I understand will not be a long one, I understand. Our rules require that before you do so, you make a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath, to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is contained in a piece of paper that Madam Usher is going to give to you very shortly. I would like you now to stand up, read out that text aloud, with the understanding that that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal, that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I thank you. You may sit down. Is the sound level of the interpretation good for you, or do you want it higher or lower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You are going, first, to be asked a series of questions by a member of the team for the Prosecution, and I think tomorrow we will then have the cross-examination which will be conducted by the lead counsel for the Defence. My responsibility is to draw your attention to the oath, to the solemn declaration you just made, on the basis of which you have a legal obligation, and also a moral one, to answer all questions that are put to you, irrespective of who is putting the questions, truthfully, honestly, and as fully as possible, as complete as possible. Did I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have any questions you want to put to me before we start, please go ahead. Otherwise, I would invite Jose Doria --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Jose Doria, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Jose Doria, to proceed with his questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Doria, you may proceed. I take it that you will be finishing your in-chief today?

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have exactly, more or less, one hour from now. Examined by Mr. Doria:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is that correct that your name is Vidosav Dzokic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct that you were born on the 9th of September, 1950?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1951. Is that correct that you are of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct that you are married and you have children?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct that your wife's name is Bojka, and you have three children?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Bojka. I have three children. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, that the children's names are Jakov, Vidosava and Slavko?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct that your mother, Radojka, also used to live together with you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct that you used to live in the village of Kalabace, Sekovici municipality?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct that you are constructor as your professional occupation?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct that you used to work for a construction company in Belgrade, since 1975 until 2002, when you retired?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how often did you used to come back home during that period?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Seven days a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was your relationship with your wife and with your children?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: It was good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to follow the schooling and education of your children?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concerning Jakov, your eldest son, did he go to the school?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Eight. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did he go to the school?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: For eight years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, that your son stopped to study when he was about 15, 16 years old?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: That's when he stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It should have been, if he stopped his studies at around 15, 16 years old, it should have been in 1987, 1988. Can you tell the Judges what --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What was doing your son after finishing his studies?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: He stayed with me in Bosnia and in Belgrade. In 1990, he joined me in Belgrade. He stayed there because he got a job with a company, Mosta Gradnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long did he stay with you in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: For six months. After that he went into the army, in 1991, on the 17th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he used to live with you, you say that he used to live with you a time in Bosnia and in Belgrade. Was he living together with you in the same house, or he was living separated from you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: He was living with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that in 1991, your son left for military service. Where did he leave his belongings when he left for military service, his personal belongings?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade, in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the next time that you saw your son? You said in 1991 he left for military service. Did he come back?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: He came back and then went -- he was there, he was captured there, and then he went to Kranj, where he was captured, and then a month later he was released. And upon his return, he went to Tuzla for his military service. That was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if all his belongings, you said you left his belongings in Belgrade, do you recall if he had any other belongings in Kalabace?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: He had his clothes and the outfit he worked in, because we were together in one household.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you stated that it was in May 1992, is that right, that he came back to see you from his military service.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: He came from Han Pijesak in May 1992, it must have been around the 10th of May. He just spent the night with us and then returned to Han Pijesak. He said that he was supposed to be released from the army in some 10 days. I was waiting for him, but he never showed up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know why he didn't come back?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: His intention was to set out for Belgrade. He reached Konjevic Polje, where he was captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you find out that he was captured?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: A courier came to me later on. He was sent by the Muslims. He came to my home, but I was already semi-conscious when he was there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: I wasn't there when he came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you got the information that he was captured, have you ever seen him again?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit P66, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Do we have the B/C/S version? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you just said that your wife's name was Bojka. Is that correct, that Bojka was also --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Jakov's mother?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, that Bojka was born in Basici?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct that your son, Jakov, was born on 15th October, 1972?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, that he served in the JNA until 7 February 1992, in Klanica and was then sent to Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct that when he left your home the second time to finish his military service he was wearing a camouflage olive-drab uniform?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. When he came to our house in May, he was wearing a military uniform. It was on the 10th -- or was it the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it with this uniform that he left your home too?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He left for Han Pijesak. He returned to Han Pijesak. He just spent the night at my place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, that he also told you that he was going to Han Pijesak for only ten days?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: That's correct, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Witness, you said that you never saw your son again. Did you have any kind of communication with him after May 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time after that event that you came to know about the whereabouts of your son?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: A courier came to my house, and I only learnt that he was captured on the 17th of May, in Konjevic Polje. But at that time I was already in a very serious condition and had to receive medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You already told us about that. I mean after knowing, being informed about his capture, did you try to find out more information concerning your son?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, Andza came from the prison in Srebrenica. She was at the Zvornik hospital, and she was calling upon me to come and see her, but I couldn't. My daughter and my wife did. And she told them about my son and how ill he was, in a very bad condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from Andza, was there anyone else who told you about the conditions of detention of your son?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: There was this man by the name of Misic. I don't know what his surname was. He was in the Zvornik hospital. And he had also come from the prison in Srebrenica. I wasn't there because I was working for my company in Belgrade. There was this friend of mine, Krsto Asceric, who is dead now, and he told him about my son, how he was in very bad shape, he was unable to stand up. And so this colleague of mine conveyed this information to me. We were both working together at the company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did Miso tell your colleague?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: He told him that he was sick, that he could not stand up in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to find out -- did you get any further information concerning your son after that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Another neighbour of mine from Kamenica told another neighbour that, apparently, this other one knew where my son had been buried, actually thrown, in a ditch. But I was unable to verify this information. And this neighbour was an elderly man who died later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I just inquire of you whether there has been any exhumation of any body that could have been --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is not receiving any interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't told about that. I was never notified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You're not aware of any exhumations. I'm asking because, in his statement, he does mention that at some point in time he was shown some clothes, or something like that, and that he could not, in any way, identify those. So if he was shown some clothes, I would have presumed for some time at least that there could have been some body that could have been retrieved and possibly -- you're not aware of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: We are not aware of anything, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Yes, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Vidovic. So we don't have the proof of that, nothing. It's just the suggestion that it could have happened, in other words. That's it. Yes, Madam Vidovic. Madam Vidovic now is going to -- yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, just one very brief matter. I won't trouble the Chamber for long. I don't want to hold the Prosecution to that position necessarily without being able to research it properly and answer Your Honour's inquiry, a very pertinent inquiry, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My remark, Mr. Di Fazio, was a very -- originates, derives from that bit in his statement referring to pieces of cloth. I don't know. They don't usually fall from heaven. MR. DI FAZIO: I know. But as you can see from the statement, he was unable to do anything with it, and that's why we haven't led evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I want to know is whether behind that is the retrieval of a body which someone might have thought for a time could belong to his son. MR. DI FAZIO: I could make that inquiry and let you know and, with respect, it's a very pertinent inquiry. If -- as I said, I don't want the Prosecution to be held to this position -- we don't intend to lead it. It may be that at some later point there would be further evidence touching upon that, and I don't want to be in a position to then say, Well, you said that previously there was no such information and now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. There's also a bit of information in a statement which refers to a possible site where the bodies of this person, plus two others, were thrown. MR. DI FAZIO: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I mean, I haven't heard any questions on those, and obviously I suppose you have taken those into consideration as well. Madam Vidovic. Cross-examined by Ms. Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you a series of questions. I believe we can finish today. Leaving aside for a moment what other people told you about your son, and basing ourselves on what you know from your personal knowledge, the only thing you can say is that you believe your son is dead just because you haven't seen him since May of 1992. And you also believe that he would have been in touch if he was alive. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on the accounts of other people, you believe that your son died in prison, in Srebrenica, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: That's what I believe. They said that he had died. There were a number of witnesses who heard -- Miso and Andza both said that there was no way that he could have survived, and that he died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dzokic. Let's take this one step at a time. You mentioned four persons as your source of information on your son, once he had been captured.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Luka?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Andza?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Miso?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A Bosniak called Hasan?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These four persons, if you look at these four persons, the first three, in fact, never told you anything about your son's death, did they?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: They didn't, but Hasan Milic from Kamenica told his neighbour, Nedjo, that he had died and that he was thrown into some sort of a pit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzokic, please, can you hear me out? Listen carefully to my question, and make a pause so that my question can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Luka was the one who told you that the Muslims had captured your son at Konjevic Polje, in late May 1992, and that he was then transferred to Cerska; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Luka said it was on the 17th of May, 1992, that he had been transferred to Cerska, that later he had been transferred to Cerska -- to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. What Andza told you is true in as far as -- the information that Andza had was true, and this is something she conveyed to you through her wife [as interpreted]; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's something wrong with the transcript. I mean, I know we are living in very modern times sometimes, but I didn't expect to find that Andza had a wife as well. So it looks as if there is some mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll repeat the question. What I said has nothing to do with that. Your Honour, I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What Andza told you is true only if her original information was true, which she conveyed through your wife.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: She said that he was ill in Srebrenica, that's once she had left the hospital and was already in Zvornik. She said that he had remained in prison, in Srebrenica, and that he was not well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Dzokic. Please, if you can answer briefly. We'll hear more about her testimony later on, and she will appear and testify. I'll just ask you another brief question in relation to this. In your statement to the investigators back in 2004, in paragraph 7, the last sentence reads: "Andza had also told my wife that the conditions in the prison were very poor. It was cold and there was nothing to eat." So my question is: Did Andza really tell your wife that they had been given nothing to eat?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As concerns what Miso told you, that was hearsay, it was something you heard through Krsto. We shall be hearing Krsto's testimony here in court, but I'll ask you another question in relation to that. Is it not true that he told you nothing whatsoever in relation to your son's death in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't say anything. He just said that he was very ill, and that he was bedridden. That's what my friend told me. I don't know about Krsto, or who told him anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you heard nothing whatsoever from Luka, Andza, or Miso about your son's death in Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I heard nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In actual fact, the only source that you base yourself on when you say that your son died in prison, in Srebrenica, is something you heard later on from a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: This Bosniak in Kamenica told my neighbour Nedjo that he had died, and that he had been buried and thrown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you never actually talked to this Bosniak, did you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. He died a month or two later, because he was a very old man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Through your neighbour, or anyone else, did you try to obtain more information as to the specific location where your son was allegedly thrown?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't go. I didn't know what or where. I didn't go. I went to Zvornik. I asked questions. I went to Basenica and to Srebrenica and all over the place, and no one could tell me anything about that. They just didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that you had information that your son's body had been buried in a cemetery close to the church in Srebrenica; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what people said. But I couldn't check this out myself. I wasn't able to find that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to request from the Serbian authorities an exhumation of that area in order to find the remains of your son?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: I did go there. I asked questions; I made requests. But no one was willing to actually do anything about it. I just wasn't able to achieve anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in actual fact, you never received any information whatsoever to the effect that your son's body had been exhumed by anyone.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you found out that your son had been badly beaten during the many months that he spent in captivity, in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: That's what Miso and Andza said, that they had been beating them. But I don't know because I didn't hear this from anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If his death was a result of beatings after he had arrived in Srebrenica, that would tally with the information that you received, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just have another question for you. You discussed your son's death with the Serbian authorities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me when I say that the Serbian authorities asked you about information related to his military service?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: They asked questions, and I answered them. But no one answered any of my queries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is also true, isn't it, that you forwarded all his personal information to the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Information from Srebrenica, Bratunac, Vlasenica, Sekovici. I went all over the place, but I received no answers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, you mentioned to them that your son had returned to Han Pijesak, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I told everyone all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a moment, I believe we have something on the transcript that was not actually said. I would like to have this clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please, my question was: If the death of your husband [as interpreted] was a result of the beatings in Cerska prior to his arrival in Srebrenica, would that not tally with the information that you received about the treatment that he received in Cerska?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV DZOKIC
utterances.text: I heard nothing about anything until Andza came along, and Miso too. The two of them came back from the prison, and that's what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Again, there is a mistake, an obvious mistake, in the transcript, page 86, line 17. It says "if the death of your husband..." And now we have a male witness supposedly having a husband. It's obvious that it should have been "if the death of your son ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The death of his son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. I would just like to say that we have raised an objection in relation to this document's authenticity, and that is the reason -- that is what gave rise to my last several questions. This is in relation to our previous filings and motions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is there re-examination, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any questions? Do you have any questions? In Latin this would have been described as a lexio brevis. Indeed it is. We are finished with your testimony, Mr. Dzokic, which means you are free to go back. You will be escorted very shortly by Madam Usher, and then you will receive all the assistance you require to enable your return back home as early as possible, as quickly as possible. I wish to take your opportunity, on my own behalf, and on behalf of Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, I thank you for having accepted to come over to The Hague and give testimony in this case. And very soon you will be left -- you will be gone. And on behalf of everyone here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's wait until the witness leaves the courtroom. That leaves us with the other witness, who I suppose is not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very understandable. We'll start with the next witness tomorrow morning at 9.00. As I explained to you, we need to finish by not later than 12.30, but I don't think we will require more than the first session, in any case, all right? I thank you all, and particularly I wish to thank you for your cooperation in making it possible to dispose of these two witnesses within the end -- by the end of the week, which would make it possible for them to return back home. I really appreciate that. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We would like to ask -- we have a request for you, and I requested Mr. Di Fazio to prepare a short oral submission in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Just a very brief matter. You know that some time ago the Defence filed a motion relating to Rule 68 and authenticity of documents, and we have duly filed our response, and now they have filed another response. The question is, would the Trial Chamber feel it of any benefit for the Prosecution to, in turn, file --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To respond to the response. MR. DI FAZIO: -- I've looked at the Rules, and it doesn't seem to contemplate the situation. I would think there's a stop point somewhere. But if you would feel -- if you want us to reply and put further arguments, we're more than willing to do so. I think that's all I wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. I personally haven't read the reply because I only got it this morning. I have it in my briefcase. Of course, I'm taking it back home. I imagine that my two colleagues are exactly in the same position. This is something that we will discuss amongst ourselves tomorrow morning, and we'll come back to you. But I wouldn't imagine. I mean, otherwise we'll be playing ping-pong here. You know, I mean, the response to the response to the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that matter, may I just say, in that sense, it's perhaps wrong to characterise ours as a response to a response. The Rules contemplate motion, response, reply. We've been through that sequence. That, in my submission, is the natural sequence, and if there were further submissions, then it could go on forever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in addition, there was a more than justifiable reason for allowing you to file a reply to the response, because there was fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Litigation has to end somewhere, as they say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, we are not pre-empting the issue. I still need to read, and my colleagues still need to read, the reply to the response, and then we'll come back to you tomorrow morning, all right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of January, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.23 p.m.,
